Jiang, Yang, Yang, Wang, Wan, Li, and Zhang

Projection-Free Multi-level Algorithms for Stochastic Constrained Compositional Optimization

Wei Jiang jiang_wei@njust.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, China Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, China    Sifan Yang yangsf@lamda.nju.edu.cn Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, China Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University, China    Wenhao Yang yangwh@lamda.nju.edu.cn Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, China Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University, China    Yibo Wang wangyb@lamda.nju.edu.cn Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, China Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University, China    Yuanyu Wan wanyy@zju.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Software Technology, Zhejiang University, China    Zechao Li zechao.li@njust.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, China    Lijun Zhang zhanglj@lamda.nju.edu.cn Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, China Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University, China
Abstract

This paper studies projection-free algorithms for stochastic constrained multi-level compositional optimization. In this context, the objective function is a nested composition of several smooth functions, and the decision set is closed and convex. Since projection onto the constraint set can be computationally expensive, we develop projection-free methods that rely on linear minimization oracles. For non-convex objectives, we propose variance-reduced projection-free algorithms and establish complexity guarantees under both the Frank-Wolfe gap and the gradient mapping criteria. We also develop momentum-based methods that achieve convergence guarantees under weaker smoothness assumptions. Additionally, by using a stage-wise design, we derive a parameter-free variant that preserves the same complexities for the Frank-Wolfe gap. Such a design can be further used to develop algorithms for convex and strongly convex functions whose rates match those of single-level projection-free counterparts. Finally, we consider finite-sum problems and derive complexities for non-convex, convex, and strongly convex objectives. Numerical experiments across multiple tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we investigate projection-free algorithms for stochastic constrained multi-level compositional optimization of the form

min𝐱∈𝒳F(𝐱)=fK∘fK−1∘⋯∘f1(𝐱),\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}F(\mathbf{x})=f_{K}\circ f_{K-1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{1}(\mathbf{x}), (1)

where 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a closed convex set. We assume that each function fif_{i} and its gradient are accessible only through unbiased stochastic estimations, denoted by fi​(⋅,ξ)f_{i}(\cdot;\xi) and ∇fi​(⋅,ξ)\nabla f_{i}(\cdot;\xi), such that 𝔼ξ​[fi​(⋅,ξ)]=fi​(⋅)\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[f_{i}(\cdot;\xi)\right]=f_{i}(\cdot) and 𝔼ξ​[∇fi​(⋅,ξ)]=∇fi​(⋅)\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\nabla f_{i}(\cdot;\xi)\right]=\nabla f_{i}(\cdot), where ξ\xi denotes a sample drawn from the oracle. Problem (1) arises in a range of machine learning applications, including reinforcement learning (Dann et al., 2014), government planning (Bruno et al., 2016), risk management (Dentcheva et al., 2017), model-agnostic meta-learning (Ji et al., 2020), robust learning (Li et al., 2021), risk-averse portfolio optimization (Shapiro et al., 2021), and graph neural network training (Balasubramanian et al., 2021).

Although stochastic multi-level optimization has been investigated extensively in recent years (Yang et al., 2019; Balasubramanian et al., 2021; Zhang and Xiao, 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022b; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang and Gao, 2025; Jiang et al., 2025b), most existing work focuses on unconstrained settings (i.e., 𝒳=ℝd\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{d}). In many practical problems, such as risk-averse portfolio optimization, the decision set is constrained (e.g., 𝐱\mathbf{x} lies in a simplex), and standard approaches enforce feasibility via projection operations. However, projections are usually computationally intensive, motivating projection-free methods that replace the projection operation (a convex optimization problem) with multiple steps of efficient linear minimization (Xiao et al., 2022).

Projection-free methods typically rely on two oracles: (i) a Stochastic First-order Oracle (SFO), which takes 𝐱\mathbf{x} and returns (f​(𝐱,ξ),∇f​(𝐱,ξ))(f(\mathbf{x};\xi),\nabla f(\mathbf{x};\xi)) for a sample ξ\xi; and (ii) a Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO), which takes a direction 𝐝\mathbf{d} and outputs arg⁡min𝐱∈𝒳​⟨𝐱,𝐝⟩\arg\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{d}\rangle. The performance of projection-free algorithms is typically measured by the number of SFO and LMO calls required to achieve an acceptable solution. For non-convex objectives, such a solution 𝐱\mathbf{x} is usually defined by the Frank-Wolfe gap (Lacoste-Julien, 2016):

ℱ⁡(𝐱)≔max𝐱^∈𝒳⁡⟨𝐱^−𝐱,−∇F​(𝐱)⟩≤ϵ,\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})\coloneqq\max_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{X}}\langle\hat{\mathbf{x}}-\mathbf{x},-\nabla F(\mathbf{x})\rangle\leq\epsilon, (2)

where ϵ\epsilon is a small value. More recently, the gradient mapping criterion (Qu et al., 2018) has also been used:

𝒢(𝐱)≔‖β(𝐱−Π𝒳(𝐱−1β∇F(𝐱)))‖2≤ϵ,\displaystyle\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x})\coloneqq\left\|\beta\left(\mathbf{x}-\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\mathbf{x}-\frac{1}{\beta}\nabla F(\mathbf{x})\right)\right)\right\|^{2}\leq\epsilon, (3)

where Π𝒳\Pi_{\mathcal{X}} denotes projection onto 𝒳\mathcal{X} and β\beta is a positive constant. Notably, when 𝒳=ℝd\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{d}, this reduces to the standard stationary point ‖∇F​(𝐱)‖2≤ϵ\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}\leq\epsilon for unconstrained stochastic optimization. For convex or strongly convex objectives, the optimal gap criterion is used instead, expressed as

F⁡(𝐱)−min𝐱^∈𝒳⁡F⁡(𝐱^)≤ϵ,\displaystyle F(\mathbf{x})-\min_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{X}}F(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\leq\epsilon, (4)

which measures the difference between the objective and the optimal value.

The current projection-free approach for stochastic multi-level compositional optimization, LiNASA+ICG (Xiao et al., 2022), combines the linearized NASA (Ghadimi et al., 2020) estimator with inexact conditional gradient (Balasubramanian and Ghadimi, 2018) and provides guarantees under the gradient mapping criterion. It finds an acceptable point with 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) SFO calls and 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) LMO calls. However, it has several limitations: (i) its SFO complexity does not match the state-of-the-art 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1.5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5}) rate for stochastic unconstrained problems; (ii) its analysis focuses solely on gradient mapping and does not provide results under the more widely used Frank-Wolfe gap; and (iii) the method is restricted to non-convex objectives, and it is unclear how to obtain improved rates for convex/strongly convex objectives or for finite-sum structures.

To address these issues, we propose new algorithms that leverage the variance-reduction estimator (Cutkosky and Orabona, 2019) to track both inner function values and the overall gradient more accurately. Coupled with a tailored Frank-Wolfe procedure (Jaggi, 2013), this approach improves the rate for gradient mapping and also enables the analysis for Frank-Wolfe gap. Moreover, by using larger batch sizes, we can reduce the number of iterations and thus improve LMO complexity while maintaining the same SFO rate. We further develop a stage-wise algorithm with warm starts and establish guarantees for convex and strongly convex objectives. Compared with previous methods, this paper makes the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    We provide the first theoretical guarantees for the Frank-Wolfe gap in the multi-level setting (Theorem 1). The resulting rates match those of single-level projection-free methods (Zhang et al., 2019; Yurtsever et al., 2019).

  2. 2.

    For gradient mapping (Theorem 3), we obtain an improved SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1.5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5}) and an LMO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2.5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2.5}). The SFO complexity matches the lower bound (Arjevani et al., 2019), and the LMO complexity can be further reduced to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) using larger batch sizes.

  3. 3.

    We establish complexity results for convex (Theorem 6) and strongly convex objectives (Theorem 7), deriving optimal SFO rates for these settings, which have not been studied in prior projection-free multi-level optimization.

A preliminary version of this work (Jiang et al., 2024) was presented at the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024). This journal version substantially extends the conference paper in the following aspects:

  1. 1.

    We develop a fully parameter-free algorithm with a stage-wise design and a refined analysis. This method does not require problem-dependent parameters to set hyperparameters and preserves the same complexities under the Frank-Wolfe gap measure (Theorem 2).

  2. 2.

    We propose a simpler momentum-based projection-free algorithm that attains the rates under a weaker smoothness assumption (instead of average smoothness), improving the LMO complexity compared to prior results (Theorem 4, 5).

  3. 3.

    We further investigate the finite-sum setting, where we can periodically compute exact function values and gradients and reuse them to refine our estimators. This yields improved complexities for non-convex (Theorem 8, 9), convex (Theorem 10), and strongly convex functions (Theorem 11).

  4. 4.

    We provide additional experimental results, including the newly proposed methods and more datasets, to demonstrate empirical effectiveness more comprehensively.

We compare our theoretical results with existing methods under the Frank-Wolfe gap in Table 1, under the gradient mapping criterion in Table 2, and under the optimal gap in Table 3, which also present differences from the conference version.

2 Related Work

This section reviews prior work on stochastic multi-level compositional optimization and stochastic projection-free methods.

2.1 Stochastic Multi-Level Compositional Optimization

Stochastic compositional optimization has been studied extensively, with most work focusing on two-level settings (Wang et al., 2017a; Wang et al., 2017b; Zhang and Xiao, 2019; Ghadimi et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021; Qi et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022a; Jiang et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025a). Multi-level compositional optimization was first investigated by Yang et al. (2019). Building on multi-timescale stochastic approximation Wang et al. (2017a), they proposed a multi-level stochastic gradient method with sample complexity 𝒪⁡(1/ϵ(7+K)/2)\mathcal{O}\left(1/\epsilon^{(7+K)/2}\right) for KK-level problems. This rate improves to 𝒪⁡(1/ϵ(3+K)/4)\mathcal{O}\left(1/\epsilon^{(3+K)/4}\right), when the function is strongly convex. Motivated by the NASA estimator (Ghadimi et al., 2020), Balasubramanian et al. (2021) used a linearized averaging estimator for tracking inner function values, obtaining 𝒪⁡(1/ϵ4)\mathcal{O}\left(1/\epsilon^{4}\right) sample complexity for non-convex objectives. This rate was also obtained in a concurrent work (Chen et al., 2021) by employing variance reduction to evaluate the function value.

Later, Zhang and Xiao (2021) applied nested variance reduction to approximate gradients and improved the sample complexity to the optimal 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}). However, their method requires a large and increasing batch size of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}). To address this issue, Jiang et al. (2022b) proposed SMVR, which attains the same optimal rate with a constant batch size, and further achieves 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) for convex objectives and 𝒪⁡((λ​ϵ)−1)\mathcal{O}\left((\lambda\epsilon)^{-1}\right) for λ\lambda-strongly convex objectives. More recently, Gao (2023) studied decentralized stochastic multi-level optimization and established level-independent convergence in decentralized settings. Despite these advances, the above methods apply only to unconstrained problems.

2.2 Stochastic Projection-Free Algorithms

The most classical projection-free method, Frank-Wolfe algorithm Frank and Wolfe (1956), was initially developed for smooth convex optimization with polyhedral domains and later extended to general compact convex sets by Jaggi (2013). In the stochastic setting, Hazan and Kale (2012) proposed a projection-free method for online smooth convex optimization, and Hazan and Luo (2016) incorporated variance reduction into stochastic Frank-Wolfe. Inspired by accelerated gradient methods (Nesterov, 1983), Lan and Zhou (2016) introduced stochastic conditional gradient sliding (SCGS), achieving SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(λ−1​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}) and LMO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}) for smooth λ\lambda-strongly convex optimization. Besides that, projection-free methods have also been widely studied in online convex optimization Hazan and Minasyan (2020); Wan et al. (2020); Wan et al. (2022); Mhammedi (2022); Garber and Kretzu (2023).

For non-convex objectives, Reddi et al. (2016) proposed SVFW, which achieves SFO complexity 𝒪(ϵ−10/3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-10/3}) and LMO complexity 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) under the Frank-Wolfe gap. Using the SPIDER variance-reduction technique (Fang et al., 2018), Yurtsever et al. (2019) developed SPIDER-FW and improved the SFO complexity to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}), at the cost of a large batch size 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}). To avoid large batches, Zhang et al. (2019) proposed the one-sample stochastic Frank-Wolfe algorithm (1-SFW), which attains the same SFO complexity with LMO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}). Beyond the Frank-Wolfe gap, Qu et al. (2018) and Balasubramanian and Ghadimi (2018) analyzed projection-free methods under the gradient mapping criterion and obtained 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) complexity for both SFO and LMO, using a batch size 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}) per iteration.

In the multi-level setting, Xiao et al. (2022) proposed a projection-free conditional gradient-type algorithm that combines linearized NASA with inexact conditional gradient (Balasubramanian and Ghadimi, 2018). It achieves SFO complexity 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) and LMO complexity 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) under the gradient mapping criterion. However, its SFO rate does not match the 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1.5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5}) complexity achieved by variance-reduced methods for unconstrained multi-level optimization. Moreover, the analysis is limited to non-convex objectives for the gradient mapping criterion, which motivates the methods developed in this paper.

3 Projection-free Variance Reduction for Non-convex Functions

This section presents projection-free variance-reduced algorithms for stochastic multi-level compositional optimization in the non-convex setting. We first state the assumptions and then provide guarantees under two criteria: the Frank-Wolfe gap and the gradient mapping.

3.1 Assumptions

We begin with standard assumptions commonly used in compositional optimization, variance reduction and projection-free analysis (Zhang et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020; Zhang and Xiao, 2021; Jiang et al., 2022b).

Assumption 1.

We suppose F⁡(𝐱1)−min𝐱∈𝒳⁡F⁡(𝐱)≤ΔFF\left(\mathbf{x}_{1}\right)-\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}F(\mathbf{x})\leq\Delta_{F} for the initial point 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1}. The feasible set 𝒳\mathcal{X} is closed and convex with bounded diameter, i.e., max𝐱,𝐲∈𝒳⁡‖𝐱−𝐲‖≤D\max_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{X}}\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|\leq D.

Assumption 2.

All functions f1,…,fKf_{1},\dotsc,f_{K} are LfL_{f}-Lipschitz continuous, and their Jacobians ∇f1,…,∇fK\nabla f_{1},\dotsc,\nabla f_{K} are LJL_{J}-Lipschitz continuous on the bounded domain 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

Remark: Under Assumption 2, the objective FF is LFL_{F}-smooth, where LF≔Lf2​K−1​LJ​∑i=1K1LfiL_{F}\coloneqq L_{f}^{2K-1}L_{J}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{1}{L_{f}^{i}} (Jiang et al., 2022b).

Assumption 3.

For 1≤i≤K1\leq i\leq K, we assume that:

𝔼ξti​[fi​(𝐱,ξti)]=fi​(𝐱),𝔼ξti​[∇fi​(𝐱,ξti)]=∇fi​(𝐱),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t}^{i}}\left[f_{i}(\mathbf{x};\xi_{t}^{i})\right]=f_{i}(\mathbf{x}),\quad\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t}^{i}}\left[\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{x};\xi_{t}^{i})\right]=\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{x}),
𝔼ξti​[‖fi​(𝐱,ξti)−fi​(𝐱)‖2]≤σ2,𝔼ξti​[‖∇fi​(𝐱,ξti)−∇fi​(𝐱)‖2]≤σJ2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t}^{i}}\left[\left\|f_{i}(\mathbf{x};\xi_{t}^{i})-f_{i}(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\sigma^{2},\quad\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t}^{i}}\left[\left\|\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{x};\xi_{t}^{i})-\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\sigma_{J}^{2},

where {ξti}i=1K\{\xi_{t}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} are mutually independent.

Assumption 4.

(Average smoothness and Lipschitz) For 1≤i≤K1\leq i\leq K, we assume that:

𝔼ξti​[‖fi​(𝐱,ξti)−fi​(𝐲,ξti)‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t}^{i}}\left[\left\|f_{i}(\mathbf{x};\xi_{t}^{i})-f_{i}(\mathbf{y};\xi_{t}^{i})\right\|^{2}\right] ≤Lf2​‖𝐱−𝐲‖2,\displaystyle\leq L_{f}^{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2},
𝔼ξti​[‖∇fi​(𝐱,ξti)−∇fi​(𝐲,ξti)‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t}^{i}}\left[\left\|\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{x};\xi_{t}^{i})-\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{y};\xi_{t}^{i})\right\|^{2}\right] ≤LJ2​‖𝐱−𝐲‖2.\displaystyle\leq L_{J}^{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2}.

3.2 Results for Frank-Wolfe Gap

We first analyze sample complexity under the Frank-Wolfe gap criterion. The primary procedure of our algorithm involves estimating the gradient of the objective function and then employing the Frank-Wolfe method to replace the projection operation. Note that the gradient of the multi-level function exhibits a nested structure; thus, the estimation error accumulates as the level becomes deeper. To control this accumulation, we adopt the STORM variance-reduction technique (Cutkosky and Orabona, 2019) to track both inner function values and the overall gradient. At iteration tt, for each level ii, we draw a mini-batch {ξti,1,…,ξti,B1}\{\xi_{t}^{i,1},\ldots,\xi_{t}^{i,B_{1}}\} of size B1B_{1} and maintain a variance-reduced estimator 𝐮ti\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i} to track the inner function value fi​(⋅)f_{i}(\cdot) via

𝐮ti=(1−α)​𝐮t−1i+1B1​∑j=1B1fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)−(1−α)​1B1​∑j=1B1fi​(𝐮t−1i−1,ξti,j).\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i}+\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-(1-\alpha)\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j}). (5)

This evaluation ensures that the estimation error is reduced over time. We then build a similar variance-reduced estimator 𝐯t\mathbf{v}_{t} for evaluating ∇F​(𝐱t)\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_{t}) as:

𝐯t=(1−α)​𝐯t−1+1B1​∑j=1B1[∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)]−(1−α)​1B1​∑j=1B1[∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮t−1i−1,ξti,j)].\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{t}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{v}_{t-1}+\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})\right]-(1-\alpha)\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})\right]. (6)

After obtaining the gradient estimation, we follow the framework of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm (Jaggi, 2013), but use the estimator 𝐯t\mathbf{v}_{t} to replace the gradient required in the original algorithm as follows:

𝐳t=arg⁡min𝐱∈𝒳​⟨𝐱,𝐯t⟩,𝐱t+1=𝐱t+η⁡(𝐳t−𝐱t).\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{t}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_{t}\rangle,\quad\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{x}_{t}+\eta(\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}).

This yields our Projection-free Multi-level Variance Reduction (PMVR) method, summarized in Algorithm 1 (PMVR). For initialization (when iteration t=1t=1), we use mini-batch averages: 𝐮1i=1B0​∑j=1B0fi​(𝐮1i−1,ξ1i,j)\mathbf{u}_{1}^{i}=\frac{1}{B_{0}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{0}}f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{i-1};\xi^{i,j}_{1}) and 𝐯1=1B0​∑j=1B0[∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮1i−1,ξ1i,j)]\mathbf{v}_{1}=\frac{1}{B_{0}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{0}}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{i-1};\xi_{1}^{i,j})\right], where B0B_{0} is the initial batch size.

We now present the complexity of Algorithm 1 (PMVR) in terms of the Frank-Wolfe gap ℱ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{F}(\cdot) in equation (2). Noting that using larger batches reduces the number of iterations and thus can improve the LMO complexity. Accordingly, we provide both constant-batch and large-batch guarantees.

Theorem 1.

Under Assumptions 1,2,3,4, PMVR-v1 enjoys the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(1)B_{1}=\Omega(1), η=Θ⁡(ϵ2)\eta=\Theta(\epsilon^{2}), and α=Θ⁡(ϵ2)\alpha=\Theta(\epsilon^{2}), we can ensure that 𝔼⁡[ℱ⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon within 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) iterations.

  2. (ii)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(ϵ−1)B_{1}=\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}), η=Θ⁡(ϵ)\eta=\Theta(\epsilon), and α=Θ⁡(ϵ)\alpha=\Theta(\epsilon), we can ensure that 𝔼⁡[ℱ⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon within 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) iterations.

Remark: (i) With constant batch size, the theorem implies 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) complexity for both SFO and LMO calls, matching the rates for projection-free single-level problems (Zhang et al., 2019). (ii) With a large batch size B1=Ω⁡(ϵ−1)B_{1}=\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}), we obtain SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) and LMO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}), consistent with the existing single-level projection-free results (Yurtsever et al., 2019).

3.3 Parameter-free Variants

Although we developed projection-free algorithms with provable guarantees, they require problem-dependent parameters to set up hyperparameters. In this subsection, we present a fully parameter-free algorithm that achieves similar rates without knowing problem constants. Specifically, we design a multi-stage scheme with stages s={1,2,…,S}s=\{1,2,\ldots,S\}. At the beginning of each stage, we reset the hyperparameters {Ts,ηs,αs}\{T_{s},\eta_{s},\alpha_{s}\}, and initialize each stage with the output of the previous one. In each stage ss, the algorithm is executed for Ts=2s−1T_{s}=2^{s-1} iterations, effectively doubling the iteration numbers after each stage. Equivalently, at iteration tt, the current stage index can be identified as s⁡(t)=1+⌊log2⁡t⌋s(t)=1+\lfloor\log_{2}t\rfloor, with Ts⁡(t)=2⌊log2⁡t⌋T_{s(t)}=2^{\lfloor\log_{2}t\rfloor}. The complete algorithm is summarized in Algorithm 2. Next, we present the theoretical guarantees for this stage-wise algorithm.

Theorem 2.

Under Assumptions 1,2,3,4, Stage-wise PMVR-v1 guarantees the following:

  1. (i)

    By setting Ts=2s−1T_{s}=2^{s-1}, B1s=1B_{1}^{s}=1, and ηs=αs=Ts−2/3\eta_{s}=\alpha_{s}=T_{s}^{-2/3}, we can ensure that 𝔼⁡[ℱ⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon within 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) iterations.

  2. (ii)

    By setting Ts=2s−1T_{s}=2^{s-1}, B1s=TsB_{1}^{s}=\sqrt{T_{s}}, and ηs=αs=Ts−1/2\eta_{s}=\alpha_{s}=T_{s}^{-1/2}, we can ensure 𝔼⁡[ℱ⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon within 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) iterations.

Remark: The stage-wise schedule matches the SFO and LMO complexities in Theorem 1 while avoiding problem-dependent constants to set hyper-parameters.

3.4 Results for Gradient Mapping

We now analyze complexity under the gradient mapping criterion 𝒢⁡(⋅)\mathcal{G}(\cdot) defined in equation (3). To deal with the gradient mapping, our PMVR-v1 algorithm only requires minimal modifications to fit this criterion. Using Proposition 2 of Xiao et al. (2022), gradient mapping can be decomposed into two components:

𝒢⁡(𝐱t)≤−4​β​min𝐰∈𝒳⁡g⁡(𝐰,𝐱t,𝐯t)+2​‖∇F​(𝐱t)−𝐯t‖2,\displaystyle\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\leq-4\beta\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{X}}g(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{v}_{t})+2\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\mathbf{v}_{t}\right\|^{2},

where g⁡(𝐰,𝐱t,𝐯t)=⟨𝐯t,𝐰−𝐱t⟩+β2​‖𝐰−𝐱t‖2g(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{v}_{t})=\langle\mathbf{v}_{t},\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\rangle+\frac{\beta}{2}\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\|^{2}. Since our PMVR method has already employed variance-reduced techniques to ensure that the gradient estimation error 𝔼⁡[‖∇F​(𝐱t)−𝐯t‖2]\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\mathbf{v}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right] decreases over time, we can reuse this part and focus on controlling the −min𝐰∈𝒳⁡g⁡(𝐰,𝐱t,𝐯t)-\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{X}}g(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{v}_{t}) term. To address this constrained quadratic minimization problem, we design a sub-algorithm, modified from the Frank-Wolfe method (Jaggi, 2013), which runs for NN loops. At inner iteration nn, we compute:

𝐬=arg⁡min𝐬^∈𝒳​⟨𝐯t+β⁡(𝐰n−𝐱t),𝐬^⟩,𝐰n+1=(1−γt)​𝐰n+γt​𝐬.\displaystyle\mathbf{s}=\arg\min_{\hat{\mathbf{s}}\in\mathcal{X}}\left\langle\mathbf{v}_{t}+\beta\left(\mathbf{w}_{n}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right),\hat{\mathbf{s}}\right\rangle,\quad\mathbf{w}_{n+1}=\left(1-\gamma_{t}\right)\mathbf{w}_{n}+\gamma_{t}\mathbf{s}.

Note that 𝐯t+β⁡(𝐰n−𝐱t)\mathbf{v}_{t}+\beta\left(\mathbf{w}_{n}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right) is the gradient of g⁡(𝐰n,𝐱t,𝐯t)g(\mathbf{w}_{n},\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{v}_{t}) with respect to 𝐰\mathbf{w} at 𝐰=𝐰n\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}_{n}. Thus, we obtain the PMVR-v2 method by replacing Step 10 of Algorithm 1 with Algorithm 3 and can provide the guarantees for gradient mapping in the following theorem.

Theorem 3.

Under Assumptions 1,2,3,4, our PMVR-v2 enjoys the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(1)B_{1}=\Omega(1), N=Ω⁡(ϵ−1)N=\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}), η=Θ⁡(ϵ)\eta=\Theta(\sqrt{\epsilon}), and α=Θ⁡(ϵ)\alpha=\Theta(\epsilon), we can ensure 𝔼⁡[𝒢⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon in 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1.5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5}) iterations.

  2. (ii)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(ϵ−0.5)B_{1}=\Omega(\epsilon^{-0.5}), N=Ω⁡(ϵ−1)N=\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}), η=Θ⁡(1)\eta=\Theta(1), and α=Θ⁡(ϵ)\alpha=\Theta(\sqrt{\epsilon}), we can ensure 𝔼⁡[𝒢⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon in 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}) iterations.

Remark: (i) With constant batch size, PMVR-v2 yields 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1.5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5}) SFO complexity and 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2.5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2.5}) LMO complexity, improving upon LiNASA+ICG (Xiao et al., 2022) (which attains 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) SFO and 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) LMO complexities). (ii) With B1=Ω⁡(ϵ−0.5)B_{1}=\Omega(\epsilon^{-0.5}), PMVR-v2 achieves 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1.5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5}) SFO and 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) LMO complexities. These rates improve upon single-level methods such as NCGS (Qu et al., 2018) and SGD+ICG (Balasubramanian and Ghadimi, 2018), which use larger batch size 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}) and have worse SFO complexity 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}). Notably, our SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1.5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5}) also matches the lower bound for stochastic unconstrained optimization (Arjevani et al., 2019).

4 Projection-free Momentum-based Methods for Non-convex Functions

In this section, we develop momentum-based projection-free methods for non-convex multi-level compositional optimization under weaker smoothness assumptions. In particular, unlike the variance-reduced methods in the previous section, the results here do not rely on the average smoothness/Lipschitz assumptions. We first provide guarantees under the Frank-Wolfe gap and then extend the approach to the gradient mapping criterion.

4.1 Results for Frank-Wolfe Gap

Although the variance-reduced methods achieve improved complexity, their analysis relies on average smoothness and average Lipschitz conditions (Assumption 4), which are stronger than the standard smoothness/Lipschitz assumptions typically used in stochastic optimization. Momentum-based methods are known to yield convergence guarantees under standard smoothness assumptions. We therefore develop a simpler momentum-based projection-free algorithm and provide its theoretical guarantees.

The momentum-based method differs from PMVR primarily in the construction of the function and gradient estimators. Instead of the STORM-type variance-reduced updates, we use exponential moving averages. For each level ii, we maintain an estimator 𝐮ti\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i} to track the inner function value fi​(⋅)f_{i}(\cdot) via

𝐮ti=(1−α)​𝐮t−1i+α​1B1​∑j=1B1fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j).\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i}+\alpha\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j}). (7)

This update is simpler and controls the estimation error over time without Assumption 4. Similarly, we employ a momentum-based estimator 𝐯t\mathbf{v}_{t} to evaluate the overall gradient by

𝐯t=(1−α)​𝐯t−1+α​1B1​∑j=1B1[∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)].\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{t}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{v}_{t-1}+\alpha\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})\right]. (8)

The remaining steps follow PMVR, replacing projections with a Frank-Wolfe update. The full method is given in Algorithm 1 (PMM). Next, we present the complexity guarantees with respect to the Frank-Wolfe gap.

Theorem 4.

Under Assumptions 1,2,3, by setting B1=TB_{1}=T, η=T−1/2\eta=T^{-1/2}, and α=1/2\alpha=1/2, our PMM-v1 algorithm ensures 𝔼⁡[ℱ⁡(𝐱τ)]≤𝒪⁡(1/T)\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T}).

Remark: (i) To ensure 𝔼⁡[ℱ⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon, we require B1=T=Ω⁡(ϵ−2)B_{1}=T=\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}). Therefore, the resulting SFO and LMO complexities are 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4}) and 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}), respectively. (ii) As in Section 3.3, the above result can be made fully parameter-free via a stage-wise schedule with B1s=TsB_{1}^{s}=T_{s}, ηs=Ts−1/2\eta_{s}=T_{s}^{-1/2}, and αs=1/2\alpha_{s}=1/2 for stage-wise PMM-v1.

4.2 Results for Gradient Mapping

We consider the gradient mapping criterion 𝒢⁡(⋅)\mathcal{G}(\cdot) in this subsection. As in PMVR-v2, we replace Step 10 in Algorithm 1 (PMM) with the inner Frank-Wolfe procedure (Algorithm 3), yielding PMM-v2. Then, we can obtain the guarantees for gradient mapping below.

Theorem 5.

Under Assumptions 1,2,3, by setting B1=N=TB_{1}=N=T, η=Θ⁡(1)\eta=\Theta(1), and α=1/2\alpha=1/2, our PMM-v2 algortithm can ensure 𝔼⁡[𝒢⁡(𝐱τ)]≤𝒪⁡(1/T)\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\mathcal{O}(1/T).

Remark: To ensure 𝔼⁡[𝒢⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon, we require B1=N=T=Ω⁡(ϵ)B_{1}=N=T=\Omega(\epsilon). Therefore, the SFO complexity B1​TB_{1}T and the LMO complexity N​TNT are both 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}). Notably, the 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) SFO complexity matches the lower bound for stochastic unconstrained optimization under standard smoothness assumptions (Arjevani et al., 2019) and is thus optimal.

5 The Proposed Methods for Convex and Strongly Convex Functions

In addition to the non-convex analyses in previous sections, we study the cases where the objective function FF is convex or strongly convex, defined as follows.

Assumption 5.

A function F:𝒳↦ℝF:\mathcal{X}\mapsto\mathbb{R} is convex if

F⁡(𝐲)≥F⁡(𝐱)+⟨∇F​(𝐱),𝐲−𝐱⟩,∀𝐱,𝐲∈𝒳.\displaystyle F(\mathbf{y})\geq F(\mathbf{x})+\langle\nabla F(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\rangle,\quad\forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{X}.
Assumption 6.

A function F:𝒳↦ℝF:\mathcal{X}\mapsto\mathbb{R} is λ\lambda-strongly convex if

F⁡(𝐲)≥F⁡(𝐱)+⟨∇F​(𝐱),𝐲−𝐱⟩+λ2​‖𝐲−𝐱‖2,∀𝐱,𝐲∈𝒳.\displaystyle F(\mathbf{y})\geq F(\mathbf{x})+\langle\nabla F(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\rangle+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|^{2},\quad\forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{X}.

When FF is convex (or strongly convex), any local optimal point is globally optimal. Accordingly, we measure progress using the optimal gap in equation (4). Next, we consider the case for convex and strongly convex functions, respectively.

5.1 Convex Objectives

First, we investigate the case for convex functions. To obtain optimal-gap guarantees, we adopt the stage-wise warm-start framework of Algorithm 2. Specifically, we run Algorithm 1 (PMVR) for SS stages. At stage ss we use a new set of parameters {Ts,ηs,αs}\{T_{s},\eta_{s},\alpha_{s}\} and initialize the algorithm with the output from the previous stage (𝐱s−1,𝐮s−1,𝐯s−1)(\mathbf{x}_{s-1},\mathbf{u}_{s-1},\mathbf{v}_{s-1}). By decreasing ηs\eta_{s} and αs\alpha_{s} while increasing TsT_{s} across stages, we can ensure geometric decay of the expected optimal gap, namely 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱s)−F⋆]≤12​𝔼​[F⁡(𝐱s−1)−F⋆]\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{s})-F_{\star}\right]\leq\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{s-1})-F_{\star}\right]. Let S=𝒪⁡(log⁡(ϵ1ϵ))S=\mathcal{O}(\log(\frac{\epsilon_{1}}{\epsilon})) and define ϵs=ϵ1/2s\epsilon_{s}=\epsilon_{1}/2^{s}, where ϵ1\epsilon_{1} is a positive constant. We can obtain the guarantees for the optimal gap in the following theorem.

Theorem 6.

For convex objectives, under Assumptions 1,2,3,4, Stage-wise PMVR-v1 enjoys the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(1)B_{1}=\Omega(1), ηs=Θ⁡(ϵs2)\eta_{s}=\Theta(\epsilon_{s}^{2}), αs=Θ⁡(ϵs2)\alpha_{s}=\Theta(\epsilon_{s}^{2}), and Ts=Ω⁡(ϵs−2)T_{s}=\Omega(\epsilon_{s}^{-2}), we can ensure that 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱S)]−min𝐱^⁡F⁡(𝐱^)≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{S})\right]-\min_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}F(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\leq\epsilon in 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) iterations.

  2. (ii)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(ϵs−1)B_{1}=\Omega(\epsilon_{s}^{-1}), ηs=Θ⁡(ϵs)\eta_{s}=\Theta(\epsilon_{s}), αs=Θ⁡(ϵs)\alpha_{s}=\Theta(\epsilon_{s}), and Ts=Ω⁡(ϵs−1)T_{s}=\Omega(\epsilon_{s}^{-1}), we can ensure 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱S)]−min𝐱^⁡F⁡(𝐱^)≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{S})\right]-\min_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}F(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\leq\epsilon in 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}) iterations.

Remark: (i) With constant batch size, the above result implies 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) complexity for both SFO and LMO, matching the best-known rates for single-level projection-free methods (Zhang et al., 2019). The 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) SFO rate is already optimal for stochastic convex optimization (Agarwal et al., 2012). (ii) With a large batch size B1=Ω⁡(ϵ−1)B_{1}=\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}), the method achieves the same SFO complexity and improves the LMO complexity to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}), consistent with single-level projection-free methods such as SPIDER-FW (Yurtsever et al., 2019).

5.2 Strongly Convex Objectives

For strongly convex objectives, we incorporate a quadratic regularization term in the conditional-gradient step. Specifically, instead of using arg⁡min𝐱∈𝒳​⟨𝐱,𝐯t⟩\arg\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_{t}\rangle in Algorithm 1, we aim to approximately solve the strongly convex quadratic surrogate

min𝐰∈𝒳⁡g⁡(𝐰,𝐱t,𝐯t)≔{⟨𝐰,𝐯t⟩+λ4​‖𝐰−𝐱t‖2}.\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{X}}g(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{v}_{t})\coloneqq\left\{\langle\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}_{t}\rangle+\frac{\lambda}{4}\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\|^{2}\right\}.

We solve this sub-problem using only LMO calls by running a Frank-Wolfe procedure (Jaggi, 2013) for NN inner iterations. At inner iteration nn, we compute

𝐬=arg⁡min𝐬^∈𝒳​⟨𝐯t+λ2​(𝐰n−𝐱t),𝐬^⟩,𝐰n+1=(1−γt)​𝐰n+γt​𝐬,\begin{split}\mathbf{s}=&\arg\min_{\hat{\mathbf{s}}\in\mathcal{X}}\left\langle\mathbf{v}_{t}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\left(\mathbf{w}_{n}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right),\hat{\mathbf{s}}\right\rangle,\quad\mathbf{w}_{n+1}=\left(1-\gamma_{t}\right)\mathbf{w}_{n}+\gamma_{t}\mathbf{s},\end{split} (9)

where 𝐯t+λ2​(𝐰n−𝐱t)\mathbf{v}_{t}+\frac{\lambda}{2}(\mathbf{w}_{n}-\mathbf{x}_{t}) is the gradient of g⁡(𝐰,𝐱t,𝐯t)g(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{v}_{t}) with respect to 𝐰\mathbf{w} at 𝐰=𝐰n\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}_{n}. Overall, we retain the stage-wise warm-start design of Algorithm 2 and use the PMVR-v2 variant with β=λ/2\beta=\lambda/2. With ϵs=ϵ1/2s\epsilon_{s}=\epsilon_{1}/2^{s} and ϵ1≥0\epsilon_{1}\geq 0, we obtain the following guarantees.

Theorem 7.

For strongly convex objective functions, under Assumptions 1,2,3,4, our proposed Stage-wise PMVR-v2 algorithm enjoys the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    Setting B1=Ω⁡(1)B_{1}=\Omega(1), N=Ω⁡(λ​ϵ−1)N=\Omega(\lambda\epsilon^{-1}), ηs=Θ⁡(λ​ϵs)\eta_{s}=\Theta(\lambda\epsilon_{s}), αs=Θ⁡(λ​ϵs)\alpha_{s}=\Theta(\lambda\epsilon_{s}), and Ts=Ω⁡(λ−1​ϵs−1)T_{s}=\Omega(\lambda^{-1}\epsilon_{s}^{-1}), we ensure 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱S)]−min𝐱^⁡F⁡(𝐱^)≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{S})\right]-\min_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}F(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\leq\epsilon in S=𝒪⁡(log⁡(ϵ1ϵ))S=\mathcal{O}(\log(\frac{\epsilon_{1}}{\epsilon})) stages.

  2. (ii)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(ϵs−1)B_{1}=\Omega(\epsilon_{s}^{-1}), N=Ω⁡(λ​ϵ−1)N=\Omega(\lambda\epsilon^{-1}), ηs=Θ⁡(λ)\eta_{s}=\Theta(\lambda), αs=Θ⁡(λ)\alpha_{s}=\Theta(\lambda), and Ts=Ω⁡(λ−1)T_{s}=\Omega(\lambda^{-1}), we can ensure 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱S)]−min𝐱^⁡F⁡(𝐱^)≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{S})\right]-\min_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}F(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\leq\epsilon within S=𝒪⁡(log⁡(ϵ1ϵ))S=\mathcal{O}(\log(\frac{\epsilon_{1}}{\epsilon})) stages.

Remark: (i) With constant batch size, we obtain SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(λ−1​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}) and LMO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}). Notably, the 𝒪⁡(λ−1​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}) SFO complexity we obtained is already optimal for stochastic unconstrained strongly convex problems (Agarwal et al., 2012). (ii) With a large batch size, the SFO complexity remains of the same order, while the LMO complexity improves to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}), matching the known single-level projection-free results for strongly convex objectives (Lan and Zhou, 2016).

6 The Proposed Methods for Finite-sum Structure

In this section, we consider the case where each level has a finite-sum structure. We first present guarantees for non-convex objectives, and then provide the results for convex and strongly convex settings.

6.1 Results for Non-convex Functions

For the multi-level finite-sum problem, we assume that the function in each level ii can be written as fi​(𝐱)=1m​∑j=1mfi​(𝐱,ξi,j)f_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}f_{i}(\mathbf{x};\xi^{i,j}). This structure allows us to periodically compute exact function values and Jacobians, which can be reused to build more accurate estimators. Specifically, at iteration t=1t=1 and every II iterations (i.e., when tmodI=0t\bmod I=0), we set a snapshot index τ=t\tau=t and compute the exact quantities fi​(𝐮τi−1)f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{i-1}) and ∇fi​(𝐮τi−1)\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{i-1}) for each level ii. At other iterations, we construct estimators using the snapshot information. For the inner functions, we use

𝐮ti=(1−α)​𝐮t−1i+α​𝐡ti+(1−α)​1B1​∑j=1B1(fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)−fi​(𝐮t−1i−1,ξti,j)),\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i}+\alpha\mathbf{h}_{t}^{i}+(1-\alpha)\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\left(f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})\right), (10)

where 𝐡ti\mathbf{h}_{t}^{i} is an unbiased estimator of fi​(𝐮ti−1)f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}) defined by

𝐡ti=1B1​(∑j=1B1fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)−fi​(𝐮τi−1,ξti,j))+fi​(𝐮τi−1).\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{t}^{i}=\frac{1}{B_{1}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})\right)+f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{i-1}). (11)

Using this new estimator, we can ensure faster decay of the estimation error with appropriate parameter choices. We also employ a similar design of the gradient estimator, such that

𝐯t=(1−α)​𝐯t−1+α​𝐳t+(1−α)​(1B1​∑j=1B1[∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮t−1i−1,ξti,j)])\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{t}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{v}_{t-1}+\alpha\mathbf{z}_{t}+(1-\alpha)\left(\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})\right]\right) (12)

where 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} is an unbiased estimator of ∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1)\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}) given by

𝐳t=1B1​∑j=1B1[∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮τi−1,ξti,j)]+∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮τi−1).\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{t}=\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})\right]+\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{i-1}). (13)

The resulting method is summarized in Algorithm 4 and is referred to as PMFS (Projection-free Multi-level method for Finite-sum Structure). Next, we state the theoretical guarantee for the proposed methods under the Frank-Wolfe gap.

Theorem 8.

Under Assumptions 1,2,3,4, our PMFS-v1 enjoys the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    By setting B1=1B_{1}=1, I=m/B1I=m/B_{1}, α=B1/m\alpha={B_{1}}/{m} and η=m−1/4T−1/2\eta={m^{-1/4}T^{-1/2}}, we can ensure that 𝔼⁡[ℱ⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon within 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-2}) iterations.

  2. (ii)

    By setting B1=mB_{1}=\sqrt{m}, I=m/B1I=m/B_{1}, α=B1/m\alpha={B_{1}}/{m} and η=T−1/2\eta=T^{-1/2}, we can ensure that 𝔼⁡[ℱ⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon within 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) iterations.

Remark: (i) With constant batch size, both the SFO and LMO complexities are 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-2}). (ii) With batch size B1=mB_{1}=\sqrt{m}, the SFO complexity is 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-2}) and the LMO complexity improves to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}), consistent with projection-free results for single-level finite-sum objectives (Beznosikov et al., 2024). (iii) As in Section 3.3, the result can be made parameter-free via a stage-wise schedule, e.g., ηs=m−1/4Ts−1/2\eta_{s}=m^{-1/4}T_{s}^{-1/2} (constant batch) and ηs=Ts−1/2\eta_{s}=T_{s}^{-1/2} (large batch) for Stage-wise PMFS-v1.

We next consider the gradient mapping criterion 𝒢⁡(⋅)\mathcal{G}(\cdot). As in PMVR-v2, we only need to replace Step 11 of Algorithm 4 with the inner Frank-Wolfe subroutine (Algorithm 3), yielding PMFS-v2. We can obtain the guarantees for gradient mapping below.

Theorem 9.

Under Assumptions 1,2,3,4, our PMFS-v2 enjoys the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(1)B_{1}=\Omega(1), I=m/B1I=m/B_{1}, N=Ω⁡(ϵ−1)N=\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}), η=Θ⁡(1/m)\eta=\Theta(1/\sqrt{m}), and α=Θ⁡(1/m)\alpha=\Theta(1/m), we can ensure 𝔼⁡[𝒢⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon in 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-1}) iterations.

  2. (ii)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(m)B_{1}=\Omega(\sqrt{m}), I=m/B1I=m/B_{1}, N=Ω⁡(ϵ−1)N=\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}), η=Θ⁡(1)\eta=\Theta(1), and α=Θ⁡(1/m)\alpha=\Theta(1/\sqrt{m}), we can ensure 𝔼⁡[𝒢⁡(𝐱τ)]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]\leq\epsilon in 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}) iterations.

Remark: (i) With constant batch size, the resulting SFO complexity is 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-1}) and the LMO complexity is 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-2}). (ii) With batch size 𝒪⁡(m)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}), the SFO complexity remains 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-1}), while the LMO complexity improves to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}).

6.2 Results for Convex and Strongly Convex Functions

We now provide optimal-gap guarantees for convex and strongly convex objectives, using the same stage-wise framework, i.e., Algorithm 2. At stage ss, we run Algorithm 4 with parameters (Ts,ηs,αs)(T_{s},\eta_{s},\alpha_{s}) and initialize it with the previous stage output (𝐱s−1,𝐮s−1,𝐯s−1)(\mathbf{x}_{s-1},\mathbf{u}_{s-1},\mathbf{v}_{s-1}). Let ϵs=ϵ1/2s\epsilon_{s}=\epsilon_{1}/2^{s}, where ϵ1≥0\epsilon_{1}\geq 0 is a constant. We obtain the following optimal-gap guarantees.

Theorem 10.

For convex functions, under Assumptions 1,2,3,4, our Stage-wise PMFS-v1 enjoys the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    Setting B1=Ω⁡(1)B_{1}=\Omega(1), I=m/B1I=m/B_{1}, ηs=Θ⁡(ϵs/m)\eta_{s}=\Theta(\epsilon_{s}/\sqrt{m}), αs=Θ⁡(1/m)\alpha_{s}=\Theta(1/m), and Ts=Ω⁡(m​ϵs−1)T_{s}=\Omega(\sqrt{m}\epsilon_{s}^{-1}), we can ensure 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱S)]−min𝐱^⁡F⁡(𝐱^)≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{S})\right]-\min_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}F(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\leq\epsilon in 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-1}) iterations.

  2. (ii)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(m)B_{1}=\Omega(\sqrt{m}), I=m/B1I=m/B_{1}, ηs=Θ⁡(ϵs)\eta_{s}=\Theta(\epsilon_{s}), αs=Θ⁡(1/m)\alpha_{s}=\Theta(1/\sqrt{m}), and Ts=Ω⁡(ϵs−1)T_{s}=\Omega(\epsilon_{s}^{-1}), we can ensure 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱S)]−min𝐱^⁡F⁡(𝐱^)≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{S})\right]-\min_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}F(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\leq\epsilon in 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-1}) iterations.

Remark: (i) With constant batch size, both SFO and LMO complexities are 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-1}). (ii) With batch size 𝒪⁡(m)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}), the SFO complexity remains 𝒪⁡(m​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-1}) and the LMO complexity improves to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}).

For strongly convex objectives, we retain the stage-wise design of Algorithm 2 with the PMFS-v2 variant and set β=λ/2\beta=\lambda/2. The resulting optimal-gap guarantees are as follows.

Theorem 11.

For strongly convex function, under Assumptions 1,2,3,4, our proposed Stage-wise PMFS-v2 algorithm enjoys the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    Setting B1=Ω⁡(1)B_{1}=\Omega(1), I=m/B1I=m/B_{1}, N=Ω⁡(λ​ϵ−1)N=\Omega(\lambda\epsilon^{-1}), ηs=Θ⁡(λ/m)\eta_{s}=\Theta(\lambda/\sqrt{m}), αs=Θ⁡(1/m)\alpha_{s}=\Theta(1/m), and Ts=Ω⁡(m/λ)T_{s}=\Omega(\sqrt{m}/\lambda), we ensure 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱S)]−min𝐱^⁡F⁡(𝐱^)≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{S})\right]-\min_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}F(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\leq\epsilon in 𝒪⁡(log⁡(ϵ1ϵ))\mathcal{O}(\log(\frac{\epsilon_{1}}{\epsilon})) stages.

  2. (ii)

    By setting B1=Ω⁡(m/λ)B_{1}=\Omega(\sqrt{m}/\lambda), I=m/B1I=m/B_{1}, N=Ω⁡(λ​ϵ−1)N=\Omega(\lambda\epsilon^{-1}), ηs=Θ⁡(1)\eta_{s}=\Theta(1), αs=Θ⁡(1/(λ​m))\alpha_{s}=\Theta(1/(\lambda\sqrt{m})), and Ts=Ω⁡(1)T_{s}=\Omega(1), we can ensure 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱S)]−min𝐱^⁡F⁡(𝐱^)≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[F(\mathbf{x}_{S})\right]-\min_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}F(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\leq\epsilon within 𝒪⁡(log⁡(ϵ1ϵ))\mathcal{O}(\log(\frac{\epsilon_{1}}{\epsilon})) stages.

Remark: (i) With constant batch size, the SFO complexity is 𝒪⁡(m/λ​log⁡(1/ϵ))\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}/\lambda\log(1/\epsilon)) and the LMO complexity is 𝒪⁡(m/ϵ​log⁡(1/ϵ))\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m}/\epsilon\log(1/\epsilon)). (ii) With a large batch size, the SFO complexity remains of the same order, while the LMO complexity improves to 𝒪⁡(λ/ϵ​log⁡(1/ϵ))\mathcal{O}(\lambda/\epsilon\log(1/\epsilon)), consistent with single-level strongly convex projection-free results (Lan and Zhou, 2016).

7 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the proposed methods on three benchmark problems. We compare against existing stochastic multi-level algorithms, including A-TSCGD (Yang et al., 2019), NLASG (Balasubramanian et al., 2021), Nested-SPIDER (Zhang and Xiao, 2021), SCSC (Chen et al., 2021), and SMVR (Jiang et al., 2022b). For our methods, we tune the momentum parameter α\alpha over {0.01,0.03,0.05,0.1,0.3}\{0.01,0.03,0.05,0.1,0.3\} and choose the inner-loop length NN for PMVR-v2 from {10,50,100}\{10,50,100\}. For the remaining methods, we try the hyperparameters suggested in their original papers when available, and also perform a grid search to select the best parameters. The learning rates are tuned over {0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1}\{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1\}. All experiments are conducted on a personal laptop.

7.1 Matrix Optimization with Low-Rank Constraints

Following prior work on multi-level optimization (Xiao et al., 2022), we conduct experiments on matrix optimization with low-rank constraints. Specifically, we consider the matrix-valued single-index model (Yang et al., 2017) with a low-rank constraint:

y=|⟨A,B⋆⟩F|2+ϵ,rank​(B⋆)≤s,\displaystyle y=\left|\langle A,B^{\star}\rangle_{F}\right|^{2}+\epsilon,\quad\text{rank}(B^{\star})\leq s,

where A,B∈ℝm×nA,B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2),⟨⋅,⋅⟩F\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}\right),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{F} denotes the Frobenius inner product, and ss is a positive integer smaller than both mm and nn. To recover a low-rank matrix B⋆B^{\star} given AA and yy, we minimize the mean squared loss function under a nuclear norm constraint:

minB⁡F⁡(B)\displaystyle\min_{B}F(B) =𝔼⁡[(y−|⟨A,B⟩F|2)2]s.t. ​‖B‖⋆≤s.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(y-\left|\langle A,B\rangle_{F}\right|^{2}\right)^{2}\right]\quad\text{s.t. }\ \|B\|_{\star}\leq s.

In this problem, projection onto the nuclear-norm ball typically requires a full singular value decomposition (SVD), whereas each Frank-Wolfe linear minimization step only requires computing the singular vector pair corresponding to the largest singular value, which is substantially cheaper (Jaggi, 2013).

In line with the setup in Xiao et al. (2022), we set B⋆=v​v⊤/‖v​v⊤‖⋆B^{\star}=vv^{\top}/\left\|vv^{\top}\right\|_{\star}, where vv is randomly sampled from the normal distribution via numpy.random.normal(). We also generate matrix AA by A=I+EA=I+E, with Ei,j∼i.i.d.𝒩⁡(0,0.3)E_{i,j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}\left(0,0.3\right). Figure 1 reports the Frank-Wolfe gap and the gradient mapping versus running time. All curves are averaged over 50 runs. As can be seen, our methods demonstrate a more rapid decrease in both criteria compared to other approaches, especially for the gradient mapping criterion, demonstrating the superiority of our proposed methods.

7.2 Mean-variance Risk-averse Optimization

We next consider mean-variance risk-averse portfolio optimization (Shapiro et al., 2021), a commonly used benchmark for multi-level methods (Yang et al., 2019; Balasubramanian et al., 2021; Zhang and Xiao, 2021; Chen et al., 2021).

Suppose we have dd assets to invest over periods l={1,…,L}l=\{1,\ldots,L\}, and 𝐫l∈ℝd\mathbf{r}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} represents the payoff of dd assets at time step ll. The goal is to maximize investment returns and minimize risk simultaneously. A suitable approach for this purpose is the mean-variance risk-averse optimization model, where risk is defined as the variance. The problem can be written as

min𝐱∈𝒳F(𝐱)=−1L∑l=1L⟨𝐫l,𝐱⟩+λL∑l=1L(⟨𝐫l,𝐱⟩−⟨𝐫¯,𝐱⟩)2,\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}F(\mathbf{x})=-\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\left\langle\mathbf{r}_{l},\mathbf{x}\right\rangle+\frac{\lambda}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\left(\left\langle\mathbf{r}_{l},\mathbf{x}\right\rangle-\left\langle\bar{\mathbf{r}},\mathbf{x}\right\rangle\right)^{2},

where 𝐫¯=1L​∑l=1L𝐫l\bar{\mathbf{r}}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathbf{r}_{l}, and the decision variable 𝐱\mathbf{x} denotes the investment quantities in dd assets. The domain 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a simplex, ensuring that ‖𝐱‖1=1\left\|\mathbf{x}\right\|_{1}=1 for any 𝐱∈𝒳\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}. This problem can be modeled as a stochastic two-level constrained compositional optimization problem, with each layer expressed as

f1(𝐱)=(−1L∑l=1L⟨𝐫l,𝐱⟩,𝐱),f2(𝐲1,𝐲2)=𝐲1+λL∑l=1L(⟨𝐫l,𝐲2⟩+𝐲1)2,\displaystyle f_{1}(\mathbf{x})=\left(-\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\langle\mathbf{r}_{l},\mathbf{x}\rangle,\mathbf{x}\right),\quad f_{2}(\mathbf{y}_{1},\mathbf{y}_{2})=\mathbf{y}_{1}+\frac{\lambda}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\left(\left\langle\mathbf{r}_{l},\mathbf{y}_{2}\right\rangle+\mathbf{y}_{1}\right)^{2},

where f1​(⋅)f_{1}(\cdot) is the inner function and f2​(⋅)f_{2}(\cdot) is the outer function such that F⁡(𝐱)=f2​(f1​(𝐱))F(\mathbf{x})=f_{2}(f_{1}(\mathbf{x})).

For experimental validation, we use real-world datasets Industry-10, Industry-12, and Industry-17 from the Kenneth R. French Data Library11 1 https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/. These datasets contain payoffs for 10, 12, and 17 industrial assets over 25,105 consecutive periods. For projection-based methods, we implement simplex projection using a well-known efficient projection method Duchi et al. (2008). Figure 2 reports the objective value F⁡(𝐱)F(\mathbf{x}), the Frank-Wolfe gap, and the gradient mapping, averaged over 50 runs. It is observed that our proposed methods (PMVR-v1,v2, and PMM-v1,v2) tend to converge more rapidly compared to other algorithms in all tasks. The loss value, Frank-Wolfe gap, and gradient mapping of our PMVR-v2 decrease most quickly in both datasets, validating the effectiveness of the proposed method.

7.3 Mean-deviation Risk-averse Optimization

Finally, we consider the problem of mean-deviation risk-averse portfolio optimization, in which the risk is measured by the standard deviation. The mathematical formulation of this problem can be presented as:

max𝐱∈𝒳⁡1L​∑l=1L⟨𝐫l,𝐱⟩−λ​1L​∑t=1L(⟨𝐫l,𝐱⟩−⟨𝐫¯,𝐱⟩)2,\displaystyle\max_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\left\langle\mathbf{r}_{l},\mathbf{x}\right\rangle-\lambda\sqrt{\frac{1}{L}\sum_{t=1}^{L}\left(\left\langle\mathbf{r}_{l},\mathbf{x}\right\rangle-\left\langle\mathbf{\bar{r}},\mathbf{x}\right\rangle\right)^{2}},

where 𝐫¯=1L​∑l=1L𝐫l\mathbf{\bar{r}}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathbf{r}_{l}, 𝒳\mathcal{X} is the probability simplex, and the decision variable 𝐱\mathbf{x} denotes the investment quantity vector in the dd assets. As shown by Jiang et al. (2022b), this is a three-level compositional optimization problem.

In the experiments, we also evaluate different methods on the real-world datasets Industry-10, Industry-12, and Industry-17. Figure 3 reports the objective value, the Frank-Wolfe gap, and the gradient mapping, averaged over 10 runs. As can be seen, our methods (especially PMVR-v2) demonstrate faster convergence compared to other algorithms in terms of loss value, Frank-Wolfe gap, and gradient mapping across all tasks.

7.4 Variants Comparison

In this subsection, we compare the different algorithmic variants proposed in this paper: PMM-v1/v2, PMVR-v1/v2, the finite-sum variant PMFS, and their stage-wise counterparts for convex, strongly convex, and finite-sum objectives (SwPMVR-v1, SwPMVR-v2, and SwPMFS). Specifically, we evaluate these methods on the mean-variance risk-averse portfolio optimization problem introduced in Section 7.2, whose objective function is convex. The experimental results are presented in Figure 4. As illustrated, the finite-sum variants (PMFS and SwPMFS) achieve the best overall performance in terms of the objective value, Frank-Wolfe gap, and gradient mapping. Moreover, the stage-wise variants (SwPMVR-v1/v2) consistently outperform their non-stage-wise counterparts (PMVR-v1/v2 and PMM-v1/v2), demonstrating the empirical benefit of gradually decreasing the hyperparameters.

Next, we compare PMM and PMVR. The PMM algorithm is designed under the general smoothness condition and utilizes a simpler estimator, whereas PMVR is explicitly tailored to the average smoothness assumption. In practice, we observe that PMVR performs better when the batch size is large. For example, in Figures 2 and 3, where the batch size is set to 128, PMVR outperforms PMM in most instances. To further investigate the effect of batch size, we repeated the experiments from Section 7.2 with a smaller batch size of 32 (Figure 5). Under this setting, PMM outperforms PMVR. This behavior can be attributed to PMVR’s reliance on the average smoothness condition. Unlike standard smoothness, which applies only to the global objective function, average smoothness depends on the properties of individual samples. When the batch size is small, individual samples have a greater influence. Consequently, sample-level outliers can inflate the average smoothness constant or even violate the average smoothness assumption. Conversely, larger batches effectively smooth out this variability, rendering PMVR more stable and effective.

Based on these observations, we provide the following practical guidelines for selecting among the proposed variants. When the objective function is convex or strongly convex, the stage-wise algorithms are preferable. When the problem has a finite-sum structure and full gradients are available, PMFS and its stage-wise variant are the most effective among the proposed methods. For nonconvex objectives, when full gradients are unavailable or too expensive to compute, PMVR and PMM are recommended. Between these two methods, PMM is more suitable for smaller batch sizes, whereas PMVR is preferable when larger batch sizes can be used. Finally, we give a concise summary below.

  1. 1.

    Stage-wise PMFS: for convex objectives with a finite-sum structure.

  2. 2.

    Stage-wise PMVR: for convex objectives.

  3. 3.

    PMFS: for non-convex objectives with a finite-sum structure.

  4. 4.

    PMVR: for non-convex objectives when large batch sizes can be used.

  5. 5.

    PMM: for non-convex objectives when smaller batch sizes are required.

8 Conclusion

In this paper, we investigate projection-free algorithms for stochastic constrained multi-level compositional optimization. Our methods improve prior projection-free multi-level results under the gradient mapping criterion and provide the first guarantees under the Frank-Wolfe gap in this setting. We also introduce a stage-wise parameter-free variant which avoids knowing problem-dependent parameters, and a momentum-based approach that removes the stronger average-smoothness assumptions. In addition, we derive guarantees for convex and strongly convex objectives and extend the approach to finite-sum settings. Empirical results on several benchmarks corroborate the practical benefits of the proposed methods.

When dealing with the second term, we have

𝔼⁡[‖1B1​∑j=1B1∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮t−1i−1,ξti,j)−1B1​∑j=1B1∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮t−1i−1)+∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]=1B12​∑j=1B1𝔼⁡[‖∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮t−1i−1,ξti,j)−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮t−1i−1)+∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]≤1B12​∑j=1B1𝔼⁡[‖∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮t−1i−1,ξti,j)−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)‖2]=1B12∑j=1B1𝔼[‖∏i=1K∇fi(𝐮t−1i−1;ξti,j)−∇f1(𝐮t0;ξt1,j)∏i=2K∇fi(𝐮t−1i−1;ξti,j)+∇f1(𝐮t0;ξt1,j)∏i=2K∇fi(𝐮t−1i−1;ξti,j)−∇f1(𝐮t0;ξt1,j)∇f2(𝐮t1;ξt2,j)∏i=3K∇fi(𝐮t−1i−1;ξti,j)⋯+(∏i=1K−1∇fi(𝐮ti−1;ξti,j))∇fK(𝐮t−1K−1;ξtK,j)−∏i=1K∇fi(𝐮ti−1;ξti,j)‖2]≤KB12​∑j=1B1LJ2​Lf2​K−2​∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−1−𝐮t−1i−1‖2]≤KB1​LJ2​Lf2​K−2​∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−1−𝐮t−1i−1‖2],\begin{split}&\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla 𝔼⁡[‖𝐯t−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]≤(1−α)​𝔼​[‖𝐯t−1−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮t−1i−1)‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{t}-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq(1-\alpha)\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{t-1}-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]

Next, we bound the estimation error of the function value estimator in the following lemma.

Lemma 14.

The inner function estimator 𝐮t\mathbf{u}_{t} ensures that:

1T​∑t=1T∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]≤\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq ∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮1i−fi​(𝐮1i−1)‖2]α​T\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{1}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]}{\alpha T}
+2​K​σ2​αB1+2​Lf2α​B1​T​∑t=1T∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮t+1i−1−𝐮ti−1‖2].\displaystyle+2K\sigma^{2}\frac{\alpha}{B_{1}}+\frac{2L_{f}^{2}}{\alpha B_{1}T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-1}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right\|^{2}\right].

+fi(𝐮t−1i−1)−fi(𝐮ti−1)−1B1∑j=1B1(fi(𝐮t−1i−1;ξti,j)−fi(𝐮ti−1;ξti,j))‖2]\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\left.\left.+f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1})-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})-\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\left(f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})\right)\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq (1−α)2​𝔼​‖𝐮t−1i−fi​(𝐮t−1i−1)‖2+2​α2B1​𝔼​[‖fi​(𝐮t−1i−1,ξti,j)−fi​(𝐮t−1i−1)‖2]\displaystyle(1-\alpha)^{2}\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}+\frac{2\alpha^{2}}{B_{1}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]
+2​𝔼​[‖1B1​∑j=1B1(fi​(𝐮t−1i−1,ξti,j)−fi​(𝐮ti−1,ξti,j)−fi​(𝐮t−1i−1)+fi​(𝐮ti−1))‖2]\displaystyle\qquad+2\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}\left(f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1};\xi_{t}^{i,j})-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{i-1})+f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right)\right\|^{2}\right]

Then, we bound the term ∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮t+1i−1−𝐮ti−1‖2]\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-1}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right\|^{2}\right].

Lemma 15.

We can obtain the following guarantee.

∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮t+1i−1−𝐮ti−1‖2]\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-1}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq (∑i=1K(2​Lf2)i−1)​(𝔼⁡[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2]+2​α2​σ2​KB1+2​α2​K​∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]).\displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{K}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{i-1}\right)\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}K}{B_{1}}+2\alpha^{2}K\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]\right).
Proof.

(1) For the first level, i.e., i=1i=1, we have:

𝔼⁡[‖𝐮t+1i−1−𝐮ti−1‖2]=𝔼⁡[‖𝐱t+1−𝐱t‖2]=𝔼⁡[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-1}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right\|^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right].

(2) For other levels, i.e., 2≤i≤K2\leq i\leq K, we have:

𝔼⁡[‖𝐮t+1i−1−𝐮ti−1‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-1}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right\|^{2}\right]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[‖α(fi−1(𝐮ti−2)−𝐮ti−1)+1B1∑j=1B1(fi−1(𝐮t+1i−2;ξt+1i−1,j)−fi−1(𝐮ti−2;ξt+1i−1,j))\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\alpha\left(f_{i-1}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2})-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right)+\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}(f_{i-1}(\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-2};\xi_{t+1}^{i-1,j})-f_{i-1}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2};\xi_{t+1}^{i-1,j}))\right.\right.
+α(1B1∑j=1B1fi−1(𝐮ti−2;ξt+1i−1,j)−fi−1(𝐮ti−2))‖2]\displaystyle\quad\left.\left.+\alpha\left(\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}f_{i-1}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2};\xi_{t+1}^{i-1,j})-f_{i-1}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2})\right)\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq 2​𝔼​[‖α⁡(fi−1​(𝐮ti−2)−𝐮ti−1)+α⁡(1B1​∑j=1B1fi−1​(𝐮ti−2,ξt+1i−1,j)−fi−1​(𝐮ti−2))‖2]\displaystyle 2\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\alpha\left(f_{i-1}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2})-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right)+\alpha\left(\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{1}}f_{i-1}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2};\xi_{t+1}^{i-1,j})-f_{i-1}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2})\right)\right\|^{2}\right]
+2​Lf2​𝔼​[‖𝐮t+1i−2−𝐮ti−2‖2]\displaystyle\qquad+2L_{f}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-2}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2}\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq 2​α2​𝔼​[‖fi−1​(𝐮ti−2)−𝐮ti−1‖2]+2​α2​σ2B1+2​Lf2​𝔼​[‖𝐮t+1i−2−𝐮ti−2‖2].\displaystyle 2\alpha^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|f_{i-1}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2})-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B_{1}}+2L_{f}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-2}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-2}\right\|^{2}\right].

Denote Υti=𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]\Upsilon_{t}^{i}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right] and Qti=𝔼⁡[‖𝐮t+1i−1−𝐮ti−1‖2]Q^{i}_{t}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-1}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right\|^{2}\right], we have Qti≤2​Lf2​Qti−1+2​α2​Υti−1+2​α2​σ2B1Q^{i}_{t}\leq 2L_{f}^{2}Q^{i-1}_{t}+2\alpha^{2}\Upsilon_{t}^{i-1}+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B_{1}} for i≥2i\geq 2. Then we can get:

Qt1\displaystyle Q^{1}_{t} ≤𝔼⁡[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]
Qt2\displaystyle Q^{2}_{t} ≤(2​Lf2)​𝔼​[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2]+2​α2​σ2B1+2​α2​Υt1\displaystyle\leq\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B_{1}}+2\alpha^{2}\Upsilon_{t}^{1}
Qt3\displaystyle Q^{3}_{t} ≤(2​Lf2)2​𝔼​[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2]+2​α2​σ2​(1+2​Lf2)B1+2​α2​(2​Lf2​Υt1+Υt2)\displaystyle\leq\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}\left(1+2L_{f}^{2}\right)}{B_{1}}+2\alpha^{2}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\Upsilon_{t}^{1}+\Upsilon_{t}^{2}\right)
⋯\displaystyle\cdots
Qti\displaystyle Q^{i}_{t} ≤(2​Lf2)i−1​𝔼​[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2]+2​α2​σ2B1​∑j=1i−1(2​Lf2)j−1+2​α2​∑j=1i−1(2​Lf2)i−1−j​Υtj\displaystyle\leq\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{i-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{j-1}+2\alpha^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{i-1-j}\Upsilon_{t}^{j}
≤(2​Lf2)i−1​𝔼​[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2]+2​α2​σ2B1​∑j=1K(2​Lf2)j−1+2​α2​∑j=1K∑l=1K(2​Lf2)K−l​Υtj.\displaystyle\leq\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{i-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{j-1}+2\alpha^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\sum_{l=1}^{K}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{K-l}\Upsilon_{t}^{j}.

When summing up, we have:

∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮t+1i−1−𝐮ti−1‖2]=∑i=1KQti\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-1}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right\|^{2}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{K}Q^{i}_{t}
≤\displaystyle\leq ∑i=1K(2​Lf2)i−1​𝔼​[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2]+2​α2​σ2​KB1​∑i=1K(2​Lf2)i−1+2​α2​K​∑j=1K∑l=1K(2​Lf2)K−l​Υtj\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{K}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{i-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}K}{B_{1}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{i-1}+2\alpha^{2}K\sum_{j=1}^{K}\sum_{l=1}^{K}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{K-l}\Upsilon_{t}^{j}
≤\displaystyle\leq (∑i=1K(2​Lf2)i−1)​(𝔼⁡[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2]+2​α2​σ2​KB1+2​α2​K​∑i=1KΥtj)\displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{K}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{i-1}\right)\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}K}{B_{1}}+2\alpha^{2}K\sum_{i=1}^{K}\Upsilon_{t}^{j}\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq (∑i=1K(2​Lf2)i−1)​(𝔼⁡[η2​‖𝐳t−𝐱t‖2]+2​α2​σ2​KB1+2​α2​K​∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]).\displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{K}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{i-1}\right)\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{2}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}K}{B_{1}}+2\alpha^{2}K\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]\right).

∎

Next, we bound the error of the gradient estimator.

Lemma 16.

Denote that the constants L1=(2​K​LJ2​Lf2​K−2+4​K​LF2​Lf2)​(∑i=1K(2​Lf2)i−1)L_{1}=\left(2KL_{J}^{2}L_{f}^{2K-2}+4KL_{F}^{2}L_{f}^{2}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{K}\left(2L_{f}^{2}\right)^{i-1}\right), L2=2​(2​K2​σJ2​Lf2​K−2+4​K2​LF2​σ2+2​L1​σ2​K)+2​L1​D2+2​Lf2​KL_{2}=2(2K^{2}\sigma_{J}^{2}L_{f}^{2K-2}+4K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2}+2L_{1}\sigma^{2}K)+2L_{1}D^{2}+2L_{f}^{2K}, we can ensure that:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖∇F​(𝐱t)−𝐯t‖2]≤L2α​B0​T+α​L2B1+L2​η2α​B1.\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\mathbf{v}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{L_{2}}{\alpha B_{0}T}+\frac{\alpha L_{2}}{B_{1}}+\frac{L_{2}\eta^{2}}{\alpha B_{1}}.
Proof.

Since 𝔼⁡[‖𝐯1−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮1i−1)‖2]≤Lf2​KB0\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{1}-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{L_{f}^{2K}}{B_{0}}, ∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮1i−fi​(𝐮1i−1)‖2]≤K​σ2B0\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{1}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{K\sigma^{2}}{B_{0}}, by setting α≤B1​LF22​L1\alpha\leq\frac{B_{1}L_{F}^{2}}{2L_{1}}, we can deduce that:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖𝐯t−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]+2​K​LF2T​∑t=1T∑i=1K−1𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{t}-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2KL_{F}^{2}}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{K-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq Lf2​K+2​K2​LF2​σ2α​B0​T+(2​K2​σJ2​Lf2​K−2+4​K2​LF2​σ2)​αB1\displaystyle\frac{L_{f}^{2K}+2K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{\alpha B_{0}T}+(2K^{2}\sigma_{J}^{2}L_{f}^{2K-2}+4K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2})\frac{\alpha}{B_{1}}
+2​K​LJ2​Lf2​K−2+4​K​LF2​Lf2α​B1​T∑t=1T∑i=1K𝔼[‖𝐮t+1i−1−𝐮ti−1‖2]\displaystyle+\frac{2KL_{J}^{2}L_{f}^{2K-2}+4KL_{F}^{2}L_{f}^{2}}{\alpha B_{1}T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t+1}^{i-1}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1}\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq Lf2​K+2​K2​LF2​σ2α​B0​T+(2​K2​σJ2​Lf2​K−2+4​K2​LF2​σ2)​αB1\displaystyle\frac{L_{f}^{2K}+2K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{\alpha B_{0}T}+(2K^{2}\sigma_{J}^{2}L_{f}^{2K-2}+4K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2})\frac{\alpha}{B_{1}}
+L1α​B1​(η2​D2+2​α2​σ2​KB1+2​α2​K​1T​∑t=1T∑i=1K𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2])\displaystyle+\frac{L_{1}}{\alpha B_{1}}\left(\eta^{2}D^{2}+\frac{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}K}{B_{1}}+2\alpha^{2}K\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq Lf2​K+2​K2​LF2​σ2α​B0​T+(2​K2​σJ2​Lf2​K−2+4​K2​LF2​σ2+2​L1​σ2​K)​αB1+L1​η2​D2α​B1\displaystyle\frac{L_{f}^{2K}+2K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{\alpha B_{0}T}+(2K^{2}\sigma_{J}^{2}L_{f}^{2K-2}+4K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2}+2L_{1}\sigma^{2}K)\frac{\alpha}{B_{1}}+\frac{L_{1}\eta^{2}D^{2}}{\alpha B_{1}}
+K​LF2T∑t=1T∑i=1K𝔼[‖𝐮ti−fi(𝐮ti−1)‖2].\displaystyle+\frac{KL_{F}^{2}}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right].

Thus, we have

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖𝐯t−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]+K​LF2T​∑t=1T∑i=1K−1𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{t}-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{KL_{F}^{2}}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{K-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq Lf2​K+2​K2​LF2​σ2α​B0​T+(2​K2​σJ2​Lf2​K−2+4​K2​LF2​σ2+2​L1​σ2​K)​αB1+L1​η2​D2α​B1.\displaystyle\frac{L_{f}^{2K}+2K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{\alpha B_{0}T}+(2K^{2}\sigma_{J}^{2}L_{f}^{2K-2}+4K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2}+2L_{1}\sigma^{2}K)\frac{\alpha}{B_{1}}+\frac{L_{1}\eta^{2}D^{2}}{\alpha B_{1}}.

Then, we can obtain:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖𝐯t−∇F​(𝐱t)‖2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{t}-\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq 2T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖𝐯t−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]+2T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1)−∇F​(𝐱t)‖2]\displaystyle\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{t}-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})-\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq 2T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖𝐯t−∏i=1K∇fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]+2​K​LF2T​∑t=1T∑i=1K−1𝔼⁡[‖𝐮ti−fi​(𝐮ti−1)‖2]\displaystyle\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{t}-\prod_{i=1}^{K}\nabla f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]+\frac{2KL_{F}^{2}}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{K-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i}-f_{i}(\mathbf{u}_{t}^{i-1})\right\|^{2}\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq 2​Lf2​K+4​K2​LF2​σ2α​B0​T+2​(2​K2​σJ2​Lf2​K−2+4​K2​LF2​σ2+2​L1​σ2​K)​αB1+2​L1​η2​D2α​B1\displaystyle\frac{2L_{f}^{2K}+4K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{\alpha B_{0}T}+2(2K^{2}\sigma_{J}^{2}L_{f}^{2K-2}+4K^{2}L_{F}^{2}\sigma^{2}+2L_{1}\sigma^{2}K)\frac{\alpha}{B_{1}}+\frac{2L_{1}\eta^{2}D^{2}}{\alpha B_{1}}
≤\displaystyle\leq L2α​B0​T+α​L2B1+L2​η2α​B1\displaystyle\frac{L_{2}}{\alpha B_{0}T}+\frac{\alpha L_{2}}{B_{1}}+\frac{L_{2}\eta^{2}}{\alpha B_{1}}

∎

The rest proof of the Theorem:

Denote the Frank-Wolfe gap as ℱ⁡(𝐱):=max𝐱^∈𝒳⁡⟨𝐱^−𝐱,−∇F​(𝐱)⟩\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}):=\max_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{X}}\langle\hat{\mathbf{x}}-\mathbf{x},-\nabla F(\mathbf{x})\rangle and 𝐳t⋆=arg⁡max𝐱^∈𝒳​⟨𝐱^−𝐱,−∇F​(𝐱)⟩\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\star}=\arg\max_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{X}}\langle\hat{\mathbf{x}}-\mathbf{x},-\nabla F(\mathbf{x})\rangle.

F⁡(𝐱t+1)\displaystyle F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right) ≤F⁡(𝐱t)+⟨∇F​(𝐱t),𝐱t+1−𝐱t⟩+LF2​‖𝐱t+1−𝐱t‖2\displaystyle\leq F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)+\left\langle\nabla F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{F}}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}
≤F⁡(𝐱t)+η⁡⟨∇F​(𝐱t),𝐳t−𝐱t⟩+η2​L2​D2\displaystyle\leq F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)+\eta\left\langle\nabla F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right),\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\eta^{2}\frac{L}{2}D^{2}
=F⁡(𝐱t)+η⁡⟨𝐯t,𝐳t−𝐱t⟩+η⁡⟨∇F​(𝐱t)−𝐯t,𝐳t−𝐱t⟩+η2​LF2​D2\displaystyle=F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)+\eta\left\langle\mathbf{v}_{t},\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\eta\left\langle\nabla F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-\mathbf{v}_{t},\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\eta^{2}\frac{L_{F}}{2}D^{2}
≤F⁡(𝐱t)+η⁡⟨𝐯t,𝐳t⋆−𝐱t⟩+η⁡⟨∇F​(𝐱t)−𝐯t,𝐳t−𝐱t⟩+η2​LF2​D2\displaystyle\leq F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)+\eta\left\langle\mathbf{v}_{t},\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\eta\left\langle\nabla F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-\mathbf{v}_{t},\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\eta^{2}\frac{L_{F}}{2}D^{2}
=F⁡(𝐱t)+η⁡⟨∇F​(𝐱t),𝐳t⋆−𝐱t⟩+η⁡⟨∇F​(𝐱t)−𝐯t,𝐳t−𝐳t⋆⟩+η2​LF2​D2\displaystyle=F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)+\eta\left\langle\nabla F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right),\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\eta\left\langle\nabla F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-\mathbf{v}_{t},\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{t}\right\rangle+\eta^{2}\frac{L_{F}}{2}D^{2}
≤F⁡(𝐱t)−η​ℱ​(𝐱t)+η​D​‖∇F​(𝐱t)−𝐯t‖+η2​LF2​D2\displaystyle\leq F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-\eta\mathcal{F}\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)+\eta D\left\|\nabla F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-\mathbf{v}_{t}\right\|+\eta^{2}\frac{L_{F}}{2}D^{2}

That is to say:

𝔼⁡[ℱ⁡(𝐱τ)]=𝔼⁡[1T​∑t=1Tℱ⁡(𝐱t)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathcal{F}\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq 𝔼⁡[F⁡(𝐱1)−F⁡(𝐱T+1)]η​T+D⋅𝔼⁡[1T​∑t=1T‖∇F​(𝐱t)−𝐯t‖]+η​LF2​D2\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[F\left(\mathbf{x}_{1}\right)-F(\mathbf{x}_{T+1})\right]}{\eta T}+D\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\nabla F\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-\mathbf{v}_{t}\right\|\right]+\eta\frac{L_{F}}{2}D^{2}
